source_text: nuptiarum bonum homines infideles infideliter utendo, in malum peccatumque convertere; eoque modo concupiscentiae malum convertere fidelium nuptias in usum iustitiae Ridenda contrarietate me dixisse
pass_a_gloss: Of-marriages good human-beings infideles infideliter utendo, in evil sin-and convertere; eoque now/only of-desire evil convertere faithful marriages in usum of-justice Ridenda contrarietate me dixisse.

lemmas.lexica: LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS concupiscentia=eager desire; Blaise Christian usage often sexual desire vs nuptiae
LS nuptiae=nuptials; Blaise Christian marriage good
LS malum; Blaise malum naturale vs malum voluntatis

pass_b_english: [He has said], in a ridiculous contradiction, that some are guilty from a good act and others holy from an evil act.
“Unbelievers turn the good of marriage into evil and sin by using it without faith; in the same way, believers’ marriages turn the evil of desire to a righteous use.”

choices.why: Julian's forensic virtue that renders to each his own, without fraude or gratia (partiality).
rejected: righteousness (Pauline overlay unless the verse forces it)

choices.why: Julian's forensic/moral fault tied to will, not a substance in nature.
Julian defends marriage as God's work against the charge that generation transmits sin.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded. Julian is not first-English.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Contra Iulianum / Against Julian), including authorities Julian quoted; Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
